A failed turbo requires turbo replacement plus a thorough oil-system flush; if debris reached the bearings, engine teardown may be needed.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: On EJ255 turbo Foresters, proactively remove and clean (or delete, per later Subaru practice) the banjo-bolt oil-supply screen at the turbo oil-feed line and keep to short synthetic-oil intervals. At the first sign of turbo whine, blue smoke, or low oil pressure, inspect the screen and oil-feed line before further driving. A failed turbo requires turbo replacement plus a thorough oil-system flush; if debris reached the bearings, engine teardown may be needed.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Document the peeling with dated photos as soon as it appears and open a paint-warranty claim (Subaru's paint/surface coverage is time/mileage limited; earlier claims fare better). For a strong case, note that the failure is adhesion/delamination (paint lifting cleanly in areas) rather than chips from road debris. If denied or out of warranty, the fix is proper body-shop refinishing: strip the affected panel to a sound layer, re-prime with adhesion-promoting primer, and repaint/clear the panel — spot-blending peeling clear coat rarely lasts. Address any bare-metal areas promptly to prevent corrosion. Consider paint protection film on high-exposure areas afterward.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose by road-testing for a speed-dependent hum that shifts with cornering load, and confirm with an IR temperature check across all four hubs or by listening with a chassis-ear/stethoscope. The correct repair is replacement of the complete hub bearing assembly (the bearing is pressed into the knuckle on many years; the pressed cartridge or full knuckle-mounted hub is replaced as a unit). Use OEM Subaru or a top-tier supplier (Koyo/NSK/NTN, which are the OE bearing makers, or Timken/SKF) rather than budget bearings, which frequently fail again quickly. Replace in axle pairs only if both are noisy. Have the tech torque the axle nut to spec and inspect the ABS tone ring/sensor while apart.

Use OEM Subaru or a top-tier supplier (Koyo/NSK/NTN, which are the OE bearing makers, or Timken/SKF) rather than budget bearings, which frequently fail again quickly. Replace in axle pairs only if both are noisy. Have the tech torque the axle nut to spec and inspect the ABS tone ring/sensor while apart.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose by road-testing for a speed-dependent hum that shifts with cornering load, and confirm with an IR temperature check across all four hubs or by listening with a chassis-ear/stethoscope. The correct repair is replacement of the complete hub bearing assembly (the bearing is pressed into the knuckle on many years; the pressed cartridge or full knuckle-mounted hub is replaced as a unit). Use OEM Subaru or a top-tier supplier (Koyo/NSK/NTN, which are the OE bearing makers, or Timken/SKF) rather than budget bearings, which frequently fail again quickly. Replace in axle pairs only if both are noisy. Have the tech torque the axle nut to spec and inspect the ABS tone ring/sensor while apart.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose by road-testing for a speed-dependent hum that shifts with cornering load, and confirm with an IR temperature check across all four hubs or by listening with a chassis-ear/stethoscope. The correct repair is replacement of the complete hub bearing assembly (the bearing is pressed into the knuckle on many years; the pressed cartridge or full knuckle-mounted hub is replaced as a unit). Use OEM Subaru or a top-tier supplier (Koyo/NSK/NTN, which are the OE bearing makers, or Timken/SKF) rather than budget bearings, which frequently fail again quickly. Replace in axle pairs only if both are noisy. Have the tech torque the axle nut to spec and inspect the ABS tone ring/sensor while apart.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the failure is delamination (visible bubbles/edge-lift plus self-actuating touches) rather than a software glitch — a reboot won't fix delamination. Options: (1) check for any active class-action remedy/goodwill under Cilluffo v. Subaru; (2) OEM head-unit replacement at the dealer (expensive and can recur); or (3) a growing aftermarket of screen-only digitizer/LCD refurbish services that re-bond the assembly at far lower cost. As a stopgap, disabling the touchscreen and using steering-wheel/voice controls, or parking out of direct sun, reduces ghost-touch episodes. Save documentation and repair receipts for any class-action claim.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose in order: check the blower fuse; test whether the fan runs on HIGH only (points to the resistor on manual systems, or the power transistor on auto-climate cars); listen for a whirring/grinding motor (dry bearings = replace the blower motor); and inspect the blower connector for heat/corrosion damage (a common failure that can also cause intermittent operation) and for rodent damage. Replace the specific failed part — resistor/power transistor, blower motor, or repair the connector/harness. Also replace a clogged cabin air filter, which restricts airflow and overworks the motor. Auto-climate cars with no fan and a dead A/C light may need control-head diagnosis.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect rear pads more often than you would on a typical vehicle (every service after ~15k miles). reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect rear pads more often than you would on a typical vehicle (every service after ~15k miles). When replacing, this is a routine pad-and-rotor job — use quality pads (Akebono ceramic is the OE-style choice on many Subarus) and properly bed them in. Ensure caliper slide pins are cleaned and greased and that the parking-brake/caliper isn't dragging, which accelerates wear. Owners who tow, drive hilly terrain, or use the car in stop-and-go traffic should expect rear service roughly twice as often as fronts. There is no recall — this is inherent to the brake-bias design, so budget for it rather than chasing a nonexistent defect.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect rear pads more often than you would on a typical vehicle (every service after ~15k miles). When replacing, this is a routine pad-and-rotor job — use quality pads (Akebono ceramic is the OE-style choice on many Subarus) and properly bed them in. Ensure caliper slide pins are cleaned and greased and that the parking-brake/caliper isn't dragging, which accelerates wear. Owners who tow, drive hilly terrain, or use the car in stop-and-go traffic should expect rear service roughly twice as often as fronts. There is no recall — this is inherent to the brake-bias design, so budget for it rather than chasing a nonexistent defect.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Distinguish diff/driveline noise from a wheel bearing by testing on accel vs coast and noting the 4x-vs-2x speed relationship, and by inspecting the driveshaft center support/carrier bearing for play and cracked rubber. For gear-surface wear caught early, a fluid change to the updated higher-viscosity Subaru rear-differential gear oil per bulletin 03-87-21 can help; a worn carrier/center bearing is replaced as a unit; a howling, worn ring-and-pinion requires diff service or replacement. Verify correct fluid level and that the rear diff hasn't been run low. Have a tech road-test to localize the source before authorizing an expensive diff teardown.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect the engine bay and under-dash harnesses for bite marks, droppings, and nesting material at the first sign of intermittent electrical faults or warning lights. Repair chewed sections with proper splices/soldered-and-heatshrink joints or harness replacement — avoid quick tape jobs on safety circuits. Prevent recurrence with rodent-deterrent tape (capsaicin-treated harness tape), ultrasonic/peppermint deterrents, hood/cabin traps, and keeping the car driven and free of nearby food sources. Comprehensive (not collision) insurance often covers rodent damage — file a claim for large repairs. Keep the cabin air intake and blower area clear, as nests there also damage HVAC wiring.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose by pouring a small amount of water into the sunroof channel corners and watching where it exits — it should drain out below each A-pillar/rocker, not into the cabin. Clear the four drain tubes with low-pressure compressed air or a soft trimmer line (never a stiff wire that can pop the hose off the fitting). On affected builds, remove assembly grease/debris plugging the drain holes. Dry out and treat any soaked carpet/insulation promptly to prevent mold and electrical corrosion, and check under-seat modules for water damage. For vehicles in the New Car warranty window, reference the applicable water-leak TSB for coverage. Periodic drain cleaning is good preventive maintenance.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: In freezing weather, warm the area or pour warm (not hot) water to thaw, then work the small internal plunger (press/rotate 90 degrees) to free the latch. For a stuck connector or 'won't release,' use the manual charge-connector release pull tab located under the hood (top-right corner facing the windshield). If the door will not lock/latch or the actuator is unresponsive, the dealer tests the port actuator motor and wiring harness for continuity and replaces the faulty lock assembly under warranty. Preventive tip owners share: dry the port pocket before parking in the cold.
